title: The Kitchen-Table Close
summary: Walk the homeowner through the claim, dial insurance from the kitchen table, and convert 50%+ of inspections into signed contracts without ever raising your voice.
body_markdown:
## The handoff from inspection to close

The inspection ended on the porch. The homeowner chose Option 1 — file the claim. Now you move inside, to the kitchen table.

This is the moment the entire deal lives or dies. Reps who freelance here lose 40% of approved inspections to "let me sleep on it" stalls. Reps who run the script close 50% on the spot and another 25% within 48 hours.

The script has three parts: **Walk them through, dial together, set the next step.**

## Setting the stage

Before you sit down, ask permission to come inside. Say it casually:

> "Want to sit down at the kitchen table real quick and I'll walk you through how the claim works? Takes about 10 minutes."

The phrase "how the claim works" is the offer. You're not asking to do paperwork. You're not asking for a signature. You're asking to explain a process. Almost everyone says yes to that.

Once inside, sit at a 90-degree angle to them, not across from them. Across is confrontational. Beside-but-angled is collaborative. Put your tablet flat on the table between you so you can both see it. Don't hold it.

Decline coffee politely the first time, accept the second. The second offer is rapport, not hospitality.

## The Claim Walk-Through Script

This is the script that has converted more inspections than any other piece of language in this course. Memorize it.

> "Here's how this works. You're going to call [their insurance company]. You'll say two things — you had storm damage and you want to file a claim. Don't say 'my roof' — say 'storm damage.' Adjusters route claims differently based on the wording. We want it routed broadly.
>
> They'll schedule an adjuster to come out, usually within 5–10 business days. I'll be here when the adjuster comes — that's normal and they expect contractors to be present. It actually helps the adjuster do a more thorough scope.
>
> If the claim is approved, your insurance will write you a check minus your deductible. We handle everything else — the supplements, the materials, the install. Your only out-of-pocket is the deductible.
>
> Worst case: they deny it. Costs you nothing, no obligation. Best case: we get you a roof and we'll see you back here in 3–4 weeks for the install.
>
> Want me to help you make the call right now while we have time? It takes 8 minutes."

Notice what this script does and doesn't do:

**It doesn't:**
- Ask for a signature
- Mention price
- Mention warranty
- Mention competing contractors
- Mention financing

**It does:**
- Reduce uncertainty (explains the whole process in 60 seconds)
- Establish your presence at the adjuster meeting as standard, not optional
- Frame the deductible as the only cost — naturally
- Position you as the helper, not the seller
- End with a tiny ask: 8 minutes to make a phone call

The close at the end — **"Want me to help you make the call right now"** — converts about 50% of homeowners on the spot. The phone call IS the close. Once they file with you sitting next to them, they're emotionally committed.

## Making the call together

If they say yes, sit beside them as they dial. Don't dial for them — it's their claim. Hand them a sheet of paper with these three things written down:

1. The phrase: "I'd like to file a claim for storm damage."
2. The storm date.
3. Their policy number (they usually have this).

When the insurance rep asks questions, the homeowner answers. You only speak if the insurance rep asks specifically to speak to a contractor (rare, but happens).

While they're on hold or being processed, write down on a notepad:

- The claim number
- The adjuster's name (when assigned)
- The adjuster appointment date

Hand them that notepad sheet at the end of the call. That sheet is the artifact of the close. They will look at it for the next week and remember they filed because of you.

## When they say "let me sleep on it"

About 50% of homeowners will not file on the spot. Don't panic. Don't push.

The right response:

> "Of course. Two things — first, the adjuster scheduling backs up after about a week, so the sooner you file the sooner the adjuster gets out here. Second, can I plan to come back Thursday at 6pm? I'll bring the claim paperwork pre-filled so it's a 5-minute conversation, and you can decide then."

Notice: no urgency lie. The adjuster queue is real — you mentioned it factually. No "this deal expires." Just a friendly, specific callback.

Reps who set a specific time and day retain 70% of these. Reps who say "call me when you decide" lose 80%.

## What goes wrong at the kitchen table

Three mistakes reps make at the table:

**Mistake 1: Talking about price.** The homeowner did not ask. Insurance is paying. Bringing up price introduces a problem they didn't have. Don't.

**Mistake 2: Bad-mouthing other contractors.** A neighbor had a bad experience? Don't litigate it. "I can't speak to what they did. I can speak to what we do."

**Mistake 3: Selling features.** Warranties, materials brands, certifications — homeowners don't care at this moment. They care about the process. Stay on process until they ask about product.

If they ask about product, give a 30-second answer and pivot back to the next step. Product questions are usually a stall, not a real interest.

## The follow-through after they file

Filing the claim is not closing the deal. The deal closes when the contract is signed, which usually happens at or just after the adjuster meeting.

After they file, text them within 4 hours:

> "Hey [first name] — appreciate you trusting me with this. Just confirming I have your adjuster meeting on [date] at [time]. I'll be there. Reach out anytime if you have questions before then. — [Rep name]"

Text again the morning of the adjuster meeting:

> "On my way — should be there 15 minutes before the adjuster."

At the adjuster meeting, you carry the photos you took, a copy of the claim paperwork, and a calm professional demeanor. The adjuster appointment is where supplements get won. We won't cover that in this course — it's its own module — but the short version: be present, be polite, have your photos, and know your soft-metal evidence cold.

## What 'closed' actually means in storm sales

A closed deal in storm sales is not a signature at the kitchen table. It's:

1. Claim filed (today)
2. Adjuster met (within 14 days)
3. Claim approved (within 7 days of meeting)
4. Contract signed (within 48 hours of approval)
5. Install scheduled (within 3 weeks of contract)
6. Install completed
7. Second insurance check received
8. Customer happy enough to refer 1+ neighbors

Reps who think the close is the signature lose contracts between steps 3 and 4 because they stopped following up. The close is the install. Don't lose focus.
key_takeaways: Sit 90 degrees at the table. Tablet flat between you. Body language = collaborative.
Run the script. The phone call IS the close — converts 50% on the spot.
Never mention price. Insurance is paying. Stay on process.
Stall = specific callback time. 'Sleep on it' loses 80% of unscheduled ones.
The close is the install, not the signature. Keep following through.

quiz.q: Why ask 'how the claim works?' instead of 'can I sign you up?'
choices: It frames you as a helper explaining a process, not a salesperson asking for a signature
It's a tactic to confuse the homeowner
quiz.explanation: The walk-through frame removes the threat of a sales pitch and earns 10 minutes inside the house.

quiz.q: What is the close at the end of the kitchen-table script?
choices: 'Want me to help you make the call right now? It takes 8 minutes.'
'Should I send the contract over email?'
quiz.explanation: The phone call IS the close. Filing with you present creates the emotional commitment.

quiz.q: Homeowner says 'let me sleep on it.' Best response?
choices: Tell them this deal expires tonight
Cite the adjuster-queue reality factually and set a specific callback time and day
quiz.explanation: Specific callback time retains 70% of stalls. 'Call me' retains 20%. Urgency lies torch reputation.

quiz.q: What does 'closed' actually mean in storm sales?
choices: The signature at the kitchen table
The completed install and a referral
quiz.explanation: Reps who stop following up after signature lose 30% of contracts before install. The install is the close.

homework: Memorize the full Claim Walk-Through script word for word tonight. Tomorrow, after every booked inspection, run it verbatim — no improvising. After 5 inspections you'll see the conversion lift. After 15 you'll never go back to freestyling.
